fullReport:
## Your Situation

At 42, you're projected to reach your $1.65M retirement goal by around age 68, three years after your target of 65. At 65 specifically, the plan shows $1,418,780 in the middle outcome (from running simulations), with a downside case of $1,252,523 if markets underperform. That leaves a gap of about $231,220 between the projected middle outcome and your goal at your target age. This isn't a crisis. It's a timing gap that's very workable over the next 23 years, especially since your 401k, the main growth engine in your plan, still has two decades of compounding ahead of it.

Your advisor's sequencing (401k match first, then Whole Life cash value) remains sound. The question you're wrestling with, college fund versus 401k, sits on top of that sequencing rather than replacing it.

## Addressing the College Fund vs. 401k Question

Here's the core tradeoff: your 401k is invested and modeled to grow at market rates (4% to 10% annually) for the next 23 years, which is why it's projected to roughly 7x from $126,472 to $910,689. Johnny's college fund, because it's held as a savings-style account in this plan, is modeled with contribution-only growth and no market return, and it only has about 10 years until he starts school. Based on its current contribution pace, it's on track to hold roughly $65,000 around that time (this is an estimate built from the starting balance plus contributions, not the plan's official age-65 projection number, which reflects a much longer horizon).

That combination, shorter time horizon and no assumed market growth in this model, means a dollar added to the college fund today does less work than a dollar added to the 401k. If you want to put extra toward Johnny, that's a values call and a reasonable one. But purely from a "close the retirement gap" lens, directing incremental dollars to the 401k, once your employer match is fully captured, does more to move your solved age back toward 65. Worth noting: if the college fund is actually invested in the market (some college savings vehicles are), its real growth could outpace what this conservative model shows. Worth checking with whoever manages that account.

## Addressing the Liquidity Concern

Your spouse's instinct to keep checking and savings liquid is a good one, and nothing in this plan requires touching either account's current balance. In fact, your Chase savings account is already on a strong trajectory, projected to grow from $10,413 to $217,413, which suggests you're already building a healthy buffer through regular contributions. The move here isn't "use what's saved," it's "once that buffer comfortably covers 3-6 months of expenses, consider sending future contributions to the 401k instead of continuing to stack savings past that point." That's a gradual shift in where new dollars go, not a reallocation of existing balances, and it should be an easier conversation to have with your spouse since the safety net stays fully intact.

## Next Steps

Two things worth focusing on: confirm you're capturing the full 401k match (if you're not already), then look at whether you have room to push 401k contributions a bit further, especially using any new savings capacity rather than redirecting money earmarked for Johnny. Second, keep an eye on your savings buffer, once it's comfortably covering several months of expenses, that's the signal to start nudging new contributions toward the 401k rather than letting the buffer keep growing indefinitely. Both moves work with your current plan rather than against it, and both are reversible if your situation changes.
